The lighthouse had been automated for forty years, but the door still opened if you knew to lift the handle while you pushed. Amelia knew. Her uncle had shown her when she was nine, the summer he painted the gallery rail and let her hold the bucket.

Inside, the stairwell smelled of guano and rust. She climbed with her hand on the wall because the center treads were worn into shallow bowls, and she counted the steps out of habit: a hundred and twelve, the same as always, though the eighty-sixth still groaned.

The logbook was where the keepers had always left it, in the drawer under the lamp housing, wrapped in a plastic bag from a grocery store that had closed in the nineties. The final entry was dated March 3rd, 1984. The handwriting was cramped and impatient, nothing like the neat columns above it. Three lines about the bulb failing and a note that the spare was the wrong size. At the bottom, underlined twice: "Tell Harris the storm took the ladder off the north gallery." Nobody had told Harris. He had found out when the insurance company called, and he had been angry about it, he told her once, for longer than the ladder deserved.
